utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Case IT-98-29/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to have the appearances starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. May it please you, I am Chester Stamp and with me is Manoj Sachdeva for the Prosecution, along with Ms. Biljana Blazevic, our case manager. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law in Belgrade, and I appear on behalf of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Good morning, everybody. I'm turning to General Dragomir Milosevic. Are you able to follow the proceedings in a language you understand? Can you hear well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear, and I can understand everything perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. Please sit down. As I said, good morning to all the people in the courtroom. As you know, this hearing is convened as a Status Conference, and I have to remind you of a few procedural aspects. This accused was transferred to the Tribunal on the 3rd of December, 2004. The initial appearance took place on the 7th of December, 2004, and as you know, pursuant to Rule 65 bis, we are to hold a Status Conference within the 120 days of the initial appearance and thereafter every 120 days. The latest Status Conference was held on the 21st of June, 2005. Therefore, we're now meeting today pursuant to the Rules. Let us tackle the issue of requests and applications. The Prosecution filed a request -- a Rule 11 bis request, and the relevant Chamber issued a decision on the 18th of July, 2005, rejecting the 11 bis application. In other words, this case will be tried by this Tribunal. As to the application pursuant to Rule 70(A)(ii), the Prosecution had filed a preliminary -- or the Defence had filed a preliminary motion on 3rd of February, 2005 as to alleging defects in the form of the indictment and we had a response by the Prosecution on the 17th of February, and the Chamber issued a decision on the merits rejecting this application. And the accused had applied on the 26th of April, 2005 for provisional release, but this was rejected on the 13th of July by the Chamber. Last but not least, another application had been filed in July 2005 by the Prosecution for the staying of non-necessary proceedings, and by virtue of a decision of this Chamber on the 26th of July, 2005, we had turned down this request. In other words, all the requests and applications were decided upon. We're up-to-date, and there is no pending application. So in theory, the trial could start very soon, but I'll come back to this later. I want to first tackle the issue of disclosure pursuant to Rule 66(A)(i) and under Rule 60(A)(ii). Mr. Stamp, can you tell me whether disclosure was done pursuant to the Rules and whether in this respect there is any problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. As far as disclosure under Rule 66(A)(i) is concerned, the Prosecution did complete that disclosure within the time limited by the Rules some months ago. The next avenue of disclosure that we have, which is ongoing, is Rule 68 disclosure and Rule 66(B) disclosure, which is again ongoing. We have today disclosed over 800 -- approximately 900 documents under the provisions of those two Rules. Disclosure is ongoing by way of the EDS system, that is Electronic Disclosure Suite, and we also delivered documents to the Defence via CDs. We have had discussions with the Defence in respect to their ability to access the material on the EDS to do their own searches for Rule 68 material, and we have been informed that those searches can be conducted by the Defence notwithstanding some -- some problems with the speed of the Internet connection. So there are, as usual, obvious difficulties in respect of some documents that fall under Rule 66 -- Rule 68(i) and that is documents known to the Prosecution to be exculpatory which are also subject to Rule 70 in that we received them with restrictions. Where we have located those documents, we have prepared and have issued to the various providing authorities the relevant request for waivers or release of Rule 70 obligations so that we may disclose these documents to the Defence. As Your Honour is aware, there have been other cases in the Tribunal involving crimes alleged to have been committed in Sarajevo where possible Rule 68 material was generated. We have done searches of these cases. We have reviewed the material, and we have disclosed, where appropriate, to the Defence. The Defence -- we invited the Defence to provide to us some search criteria that might assist us to focus our searches of the material which is not on the general EDS which is accessible to the Defence. There are security-related documents and Rule 70 documents which the Defence would not be able to search themselves. So in searching these documents for Rule 68 material, sometimes -- not sometimes, at all times it would be helpful if we had guidance from the Defence. The Defence has indicated that this guidance is forthcoming. However, we have formulated our own search criteria to locate potential Rule 68 documents, and the -- and we are conducting searches of this material. We have, of course, as is usual, have serious limitations in respect to resources, but as the search results are provided we review them and disclose, as appropriate, to the Defence. As I indicated, in total almost a thousand, 900 documents has been disclosed, and the Prosecution will continue to do so according to the Rules. There are no deadlines current that the Prosecution has not met, and all disclosure which is not -- which does not involve a deadline we continue to do so within the strictures of available resources. May it please you. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Stamp. You've answered regarding the 66 and Rule 68 material, and you even spoke about the documents you might have under Rule 70. These are very relevant matters. I'd like to know what the Defence wants to say. Has they received these thousand documents? Do they still have problems? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can indeed confirm that several months ago, that is to say, more or less prior to the last Status Conference, we started getting materials that my honourable colleague, Mr. Stamp, has referred to, and I believe that this sort of cooperation within this framework between us and the Prosecution has been proceeding all right so far, but I have to make a couple of points. Yesterday, I received a comprehensive document, that is to say, several CDs, and I looked at them, and I realised that they contained very important matters. But it is a fact that as a Defence lawyer I have so far been receiving materials relating to other cases - Milosevic, Galic, and Halilovic - and the only new additional aspect is that I have indeed received ten documents according to Rule 70. I don't know whether that refers to the other cases or not, but I did receive that. As you know, the indictment was confirmed back in 1998. My client has been in prison for a year already. But I must stress that so far, until this very moment we have not, strictly speaking, received a single document on the basis of Rule 62(A). So yes, indeed, we have received a great deal of material as the Prosecution has said according to Rule 66(B) and Rule 68, but of course we are conducting searches on the EDS, but this is an enormous amount of material, and things are not going as we would have expected because we would need a whole team of people who might then have enough time on their hands and be able to discover what might be useful. But we believe we should get everything according to Rule 62(A), and also the indications as to what witnesses are going to be providing evidence according to Rule 92 bis. And that would be indispensable in order for us to prepare for the trial properly. And I think that in this respect the Chamber might help us along in our communication in order to be able to prepare for the actual trial as swiftly as possible, because it will be easier if, for example, the Chamber were able to set a deadline by which the Prosecution should act in line with 66(A)(ii). At this stage, this is all I have to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. You mentioned something that I wanted to come to later on, but let's deal with it straight away. You have just said that the Prosecution had failed to disclose Rule 66(A)(ii) documents. So the copies of statements taken by all the witnesses the Prosecution wants to call, as well as statements under Rule 92 bis. As to this very precise part, if I remember well, when the indictment was confirmed I was not the Confirming Judge, but there was bound to be -- I'm going to explain to you as things are done at the confirming stage. The Prosecution will file a request for confirmation of the indictment, and enclosed are a series of documents. Sometimes there are hundreds, even thousands of documents. And if I remember well, most of the time the witness statements, the prior statements, are included, even statements by the accused if he or she has been interviewed. So here I am a bit surprised to hear from you that close to one year after General Milosevic has been transferred you still have no copies of such statements. Mr. Stamp, why? Why were these witness statements not disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Your Honour, if I might just clarify what I think my learned colleague is saying and respond directly to the question. I think my learned colleague is saying that he has not received statements, strictly speaking, pursuant to the terms of Rule 66(A)(ii). That is, witness statements that -- or statements of witnesses that are on the Prosecution's witness list provided within a time frame set by the Judge, the Presiding Judge. There are statements of witnesses which are compilated with the indictment when it was sent for confirmation. All of those statements were disclosed to my friend within 30 days. There are 64 other statements of witnesses which have been disclosed to the Defence as well. Most, probably of those statements will -- may I repeat myself. Most or probably all of those witnesses will be persons that the Prosecution intend to call to testify. However, we have not disclosed, strictly speaking, pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) because we had not reached the stage in proceedings as yet with the 11 bis proceedings and the other motions which were before the Court. We had not reached the stage yet where the deadlines were set. Notwithstanding that, we disclose these -- I think there are 64 statements disclosed, plus another ten of international witnesses that we intended to call. There will, of course, and I think perhaps I might address at this stage, there will of course be difficulties in terms of the time period for the Prosecution to -- to complete a full witness list, because as has been indicated, the matter -- the indictment was confirmed in 1998, and it has taken a significant degree of time between that time and the time when the accused came before the court, and we need to put together significant investigative resources to locate these witnesses, many of whom are international figures, many of whom will have moved. Some might not be with us anymore. But we need to contact many of these persons, and it will of course take significant resources to do so. But insofar as their statements exist and are in the possession of the Prosecution, we have delivered them to the Defence. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you answered as to the point of law, and you said that you had already disclosed a large number of witness statements, but there are some still that you have not yet disclosed because you are waiting under Rule 65 ter (E) from the Chamber an order as to the witness list. So this brings me to other equally important problems. I want first to tell the parties how things are going with the Chamber. You know that this case was assigned to Chamber II. I'm part of Chamber II, Trial Chamber II. It is composed of Judge Agius, Judge Parker, and myself. Some days ago the Security Council adopted a Resolution whereby it has been decided that an ad Litem judge who has been elected permanent Judge will start early as such because a trial started this week, and the said Judge has been assigned to Trial Chamber II. So to date there are now four permanent Judges in Trial Chamber II, whereas by Statute we should only have three, which means that one of the four permanent Judges will have to swap Trial Chambers, go to another Trial Chamber. It may be me or Judge Agius or Judge Parker or this new Judge who has been recently appointed. But it is rather likely that I might be the one, inasmuch as Judge Parker is the -- and Judge Agius and this new female Judge are in trial, which is not my case, hearing cases. There will be another event which will have a major impact on the life of this Tribunal. On the 7th of November, the Judges are meeting in order to elect their new president and their new vice-president. Depending on the outcome of this election, there may be changes accordingly. Anyway, this case assigned to Trial Chamber II might, in theory, might be given to another Trial Chamber if need be. Things might even get more complicated if the Tribunal notes that some cases are sort of lagging behind in the schedules. A working group has been set up under the presence of Judge Bonomy, and this working group has issued a report to the Plenary meeting of the Tribunal, and it is recommended in this report that the Pre-Trial Judge should get more involved in the pre-trial phase of the cases in order to speed up the proceedings. Therefore, the Pre-Trial Judge will have to exert more pressure on the parties, especially when it comes to disclosure of material. On the other hand, I observe that with regard to this case, everything is just about ready, trial ready. Pursuant to Rule 66 ter, I am now under the obligation to make a decision with regard to the Prosecution. I'm going to read to you 66 ter (E) which tells you how things are going to go. Once they are settled, once all the preliminary motions are settled under Rule 72, which is the case, the Pre-Trial Judge, following a report by a senior legal officer, will tell the Prosecutor to file within a deadline assigned by the Judge and at the latest six weeks before the Pre-Trial Conference under the relevant article will have to have a final pre-trial brief, the witness list, so the list of witnesses that the Prosecution intend to call with names and pseudonyms of each of the witnesses, a summary of the facts testified to, the summary of the points mentioned in the testimony, the overall amount of witnesses as well as the number of witnesses who are going to testify to specific counts of the indictment, and then the likely duration of the testimony of each and every witness as well as the likely duration of the Prosecution evidence. Thirdly, and I'll come back to that later on, you need to have a list of exhibits, and I see today that the accused is here in The Hague and has been in The Hague, in a few weeks' time, for nearly a year, and of course the accused is entitled to a speedy trial, a trial that is going to take place as quickly as possible, and on the other hand I see that the case is trial ready. Therefore, I'm turning to the Prosecution. Can you tell me when in your view you will be able to give -- to file the pre-trial brief; secondly, the witness list; and thirdly, the list of exhibits? Just a while ago, the Prosecution said that they had problems because the indictment was issued in 1998. So nearly seven years ago. And in the schedules of the indictment, there are maybe witnesses that are no more with us, that you have to find. I can understand that within a span of seven years the Prosecution must have been able to get prepared for the trial. So if you need to look for witnesses, you have to tell me which one you're looking for, because as far as I can see there are necessary witnesses. You mentioned 64 of them, but they are the ones whose names are mentioned in the indictment. They were wounded, and they're able to testify here as victims. So of course, normally speaking, you must know where these people are. And if among them there are people who are no longer with us, well, you can't find them anyway. And then you also have expert witnesses, and it shouldn't be too difficult to know which of them are coming to testify. I'll come back to at that later on too. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And as to the exhibit list, you have already disclosed a number of exhibits and now you should finalise your list. So, Mr. Stamp, taking into account your difficulties and problems, when do you think you will be able to meet the provisions of 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The problems that Your Honour referred to are problems that will take significant amounts of resources to gather together to deal with. The problems of witness re-contact is not a simple one. The problems of replacing witnesses where they are no longer available will take a significant period of investigative effort. As Your Honour is aware, the Prosecution did at one stage ask that all non-essential proceedings in this matter be postponed pending the Rule 11 bis hearing. It is subsequent to that and at this present time that we are now engaged and the work continues in getting together the material to satisfy the requirements. While I would not at this stage be able to give Your Honour a precise date as to when the Prosecution might be able to do so, I -- and while I recognise that the accused has been in custody for -- since December last year, the Prosecution points out that the Court ought to take into consideration the scheduling arrangements in respect to the three mega-trials which are expected to start in the coming year. That is, the three trials involving multiple accused. And therefore, the Prosecution would have to shift resource or at least allocate resources in respect of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Stamp, I understand perfectly what your problems are, but there's one thing I'd like to know first of all. You represent Madam Prosecutor. In this case, how many of you are there? I can see two of you here, but altogether how many attorneys are there? How many members are there in your Prosecution? You are the head of the team, but how many of you are there altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the entire OTP or in respect of this case? I'm not sure what Your Honour is asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, only for this case. Only two, three, or four? How many of you together on this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On this case we have limited resources, but without disclosing precisely what the personnel resources are, we are putting together a full team. There are presently two lawyers dedicated to this case full time. We will need substantially more than that. The resources that we will deploy in particular cases I would not want to go into details on that, but just to let Your Honour have an understanding of the limitations there are in respect to resources, and I think these matters ought to be considered. The schedules of forthcoming trials for the Tribunal that we have to dedicate resources to have to be put in the balance in respect of setting these deadlines. And the Prosecution is no doubt aware that the accused has been in custody since December, and we respect his right to a fair trial, and we will do everything possible within a reasonable time set by the Court to ensure that the filings, the lists and all the requirements of Rule 65 ter are met. As to a precise timing, I could not supply one, but it will, in my estimation, take several months before we have contacted all of these witnesses, determined who is able to come, who we need to do 92 bis declarations in respect to, who we need to replace and therefore we need to search and find other witnesses and take statements from them, who needs protective measures and therefore we need to apply to the Court for protective measures. There are huge undertakings that we need to discharge before we would be in a position to provide a final list of witnesses. And of course the pre-trial brief would to a great extent depend on this final list. So I ask Your Honour to take all of those matters into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you properly, you are telling me that you are currently with two lawyers, but lawyers work with investigating teams, with investigators. Presently do you have investigators available to you, and can they, for instance, if they have addresses, witnesses' addresses, can they look them up or do you have to go through legal cooperation, district cooperation with Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you enlighten me on this? Do you have an investigating team at your disposal today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Today we are engaging an investigative team. It is not fully composed. It is not fully manned as yet. But I would not again wish to get into details in matters which -- which are in a flux, which at present we are organising, because my answers will not have the precision that I want to give to the Court. Contacting witnesses, in some cases it might well be a simple matter of the normal cooperation between states. However, the experience has been that in respect to these states where there were these wars in the 1990s, many of the witnesses have moved to a variety of places. They are scattered all over the world. International witnesses do not necessarily work where they -- where they originally were working, and many of them we will have to contact the organisations to obtain waivers in respect to whether or not they can give further statements or information if we need to interview new international witnesses. And I don't wish to belabour the point as if I'm giving the Court an inventory of problems. There will be problems, and we will undertake to overcome these problems and we will do so in a reasonable time. However, I just ask the Court to bear in mind in deciding, as the Court must do, in setting a time framework for us to comply with these obligations. It is -- I repeat, it would be matter of several months before the Prosecution would be in a position to adequately fulfil these obligations. And it would not prejudice the accused, because having regard to the scheduling of cases in the forthcoming here, it is unlikely that this case will get off then, and the Prosecution resources will have to, of course, take those cases into consideration. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. If my understanding is correct, you're telling me that you need several months. Right. This is the Prosecution's position. I have to stick by the Rules. As a Pre-Trial Judge, I'm obliged - legally and morally obliged - to make sure that the accused present here does not stay in prison without trial for months or years. This is an essential right of every accused to be able to have a swift trial. This applies to all countries in the world and all the more so to international justice. You are telling me that three important trials are going to mobilise the resources of the Prosecution. We are well aware of the fact that there will be trials where there will be joinders of cases, and I myself am supposed to be the Presiding Judge on one of those trials as well. But all this was predictable. It does not come out of the blue from one day to the next. It was predictable that there would be a joinder of cases and that such trials would commence, and there are people who are being temporarily detained and they are awaiting trial. Some people have been professionally released as well whilst awaiting trial, and as far as I can see, there is a problem of resources. Now, what about resources? Is it staff? And in that case, what staff? The investigators or people present here, case managers, et cetera? I can see that the Defence team consists of one person only, and I would like to ask them whether they will continue to act that way -- in that way or will there be another lawyer present. And you have two people at the moment. So now I have to set a certain number of deadlines. I will very soon make a decision on a deadline in order to sort all this out. I suppose there might be problems. But if I refer to annex 3 of the indictment, for example, if you take a look at annex 3 of the indictment, you can see that it is a list of persons who have been wounded or killed. Top of the list is a woman who is 43 years old, who sustained a thigh injury in other right thigh as she was riding on a tram. And then there was somebody else who -- she would now have about -- she would now be 53 years of age. So either she's still in Sarajevo or else she has left. But if you contact the local authorities, you will be able to find out this woman's address pretty swiftly in order to call her as a witness. The second one, a young man, 16 years old, who was killed, but this young boy probably had parents. So if you wish to establish his family situation, you can always call his parents. On the 8th of November, a 59-year-old woman who sustained a hand injury. It shouldn't be too difficult to find her, and so on and so forth. So if we go through the list, what you have to do is contact the local authorities, submit the list, and ask for these people's addresses. In annex 4, there is what we call bombings or the shellings. The first shelling refers to a shell which landed on the 30th of October on a group of civilians waiting for a bus. It was a 120-millimetre shell. Perhaps you could invite a witness. The witness could come and tell us about these events. Since there was a group of civilians, we can imagine that there would be hearings for those witnesses, et cetera, and so on and so forth. What I'm trying to say is that this is not so difficult. You have referred to international witnesses that need to be found because they may have switched jobs and moved to another place, et cetera. It is indeed true. There are indeed witnesses that may have switched jobs, but initially we have this list, and if you encounter difficulties in getting the witnesses to come, the Trial Chamber can help you out. It is not an impossible task, after all. It is not something which is beyond the capacity of a Prosecution team. And now I'm looking at the Defence, and I would like to know what your point of view is, because you will have heard that the Prosecution would like to be granted several months to complete the job. Now, I give the floor to the Defence because I would like to know what their point of view on this matter is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. My point of view as the Defence counsel of Dragomir Milosevic is very clear. The Statute, the Rules, and the entire procedure must take account of the fact that the trial must take place as swiftly as possible, and it must be a fair and a just trial, and that of course means that we must get evidence as soon as possible, the evidence that is the basis of the indictment, because I cannot but repeat your own words, and this has been my conviction from the very start. The indictment was first issued in 1998, and I can't help myself. I just have to say this: I simply can't believe that the Prosecution is still wandering around looking for evidence. And this basic evidence that is the basis of the indictment, not just the accompanying facts and the facts that have been submitted when the indictment was confirmed, but everything else on the basis of which the responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic is to be established. Well, of course the suffering of the victims is the one thing. This is not arguable. But fundamental issues having to do with his responsibility are quite another matter. And of course we have to be able to have an insight into what the basis of their evidence is. I mean, I'm deeply convinced that this is the way in which these things should be done. We should know as soon as possible what these matters are, quite apart from any difficulties having to do with the Trial Chambers available or other logistical issues that Chambers and their make-up, et cetera. Quite apart from that, at any given moment we must make sure that the Judges get the opportunity to prepare properly and thoroughly as soon as possible. And then of course we have the technical issues, Trial Chambers and so on and so forth. That is quite another matter. But we must deal with these things with the assumption that the trial is going to start very soon. That's my basic attitude as Defence counsel. There is nothing else I can say. I am in touch with the Prosecution, and on a number of occasions I have insisted on this. And I must say that we had fairly good cooperation. We understand -- we sometimes don't speak the same language. That might be a problem. But I'm going to make an effort myself and have as much understanding as possible for the situation of the Prosecution, but I must assume that the trial will start as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to put a question to you. I see that you are alone as Defence counsel for General Milosevic. Are you going to remain the only one throughout the trial or are you going to ask for a co-counsel? The reason I'm telling you this is that in a case that is very close to this one, the Galic case, there were two lawyers in the Defence team. Are you going to remain alone or are you going to have somebody with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course it's impossible to do this completely by myself, and I am availing myself of all the possibilities under the Rules. At this point in time I do have a co-counsel. That is a lawyer from Paris, Branislava Isailovic. She is originally from Serbia but has been practising law in Paris for the past 15 years. So she will be my co-counsel. Of course I already have my own legal assistant in Belgrade, and I also have an investigator. We have just been granted the funds to engage another investigator. But other than that, of course I will have to rely on other colleagues. However, electronic searches are a lot of work. It's very difficult to deal with that and to search for documents through millions of documents in order to find something that would be relevant to this case. This is something that we will try our best to do, but this will pose a major problem, and this is something that we might have to discuss with you later at Status Conferences. I will not be alone, however. I am alone today because there was no need also in the past Status Conferences to have somebody here with me present, but of course they are helping me, and the time will come when they will come also to the courtroom to assist me. That is certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. As I stated earlier on, I am going to issue an order to set deadlines for the disclosure of exhibits pursuant to this subrule (E). Another thing that I wanted to mention in this Status Conference, because that's the purpose of such a conference, the other elements relevant to the trial proceedings. There is a major question in any proceedings. It is the way in which the Prosecution are going to present their evidence. Sometimes there is a certain degree of confusion. One doesn't understand why such a witness will appear rather than another one. So sometimes, you know, you are a bit lost as a Judge. And I think it is essential for a case to be clear and for the Judges to be well-informed, for the Defence to be able to cross-examine usefully. Whenever the Prosecution are going to adduce evidence, they should do so in keeping with the chronology or the logics of the indictment. You just have to follow the indictment in doing so, because you have a general framework, the context or background in the indictment. So you'll have witnesses who will appear as to the background. Thereafter, come the issues of liability, individual liability under 7(1) or 7(3) of the Statute. And then you come to the facts of the case which are the various counts in the indictment. And in this case, it is the terror that was spread and the issue of sniper fire directed at civilians, as well as the issue of the shellings. So there is quite some consistency or logics to be followed. As far as I'm concerned, I will be following very closely the filings by the Prosecution regarding the witness list. I want to see in which order the witnesses will appear so that the trial can be conducted in the best way possible. Also, in trial the issue of the admissibility of evidence is bound to arise. In an initial stage, when the Prosecution examine their witnesses in chief they will introduce exhibits, and of course the Defence, when cross-examining the witness or witnesses, can ask for evidence to be adduced. The admissibility of evidence sometimes raises problems, and this will cause a trial to be delayed or to last longer because there's an objection. The Defence will say that this or that item or exhibit is not relevant. So in this matter, I am planning to give this to the Prosecution but also to the Defence because of course the Defence will be in a position in the Defence case to introduce evidence. I am planning, as I said, to take up what Judge Agius stated in various decisions and orders as to the admissibility of evidence. I believe that a piece -- an exhibit should be admitted if it is relevant as to the facts and if it is reliable. Of course if the Defence would believe that an exhibit is forged or irrelevant, they have the time to challenge it. But if you challenge an exhibit at the beginning of trial proceedings whilst you don't have all the ins and outs, at that stage of the proceedings that may cause problems. I am permanently in favour of this: When the Defence write their exhibit lists as under 65 ter (E)(iii), so the Prosecution intends to say how many exhibits they intend to seek to adduce, and in this list there should be explicit references, clear references to the witnesses about to testify with the said exhibits, and in this overall list the exhibits Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. should be mentioned also with regard to the pre-trial brief and to the indictment. In this way, when the Prosecution seeks to adduce an exhibit during testimony it will be clearly identified by both the Trial Chamber and the Defence. This is far from being complicated. It can be done easily, without any problem. So you will have a written decision on this matter from me. There is something else I wanted to raise ex officio. It is the issue of expert witnesses. Both Prosecution and Defence will call expert witnesses. If I cast my mind back to the Galic trial, there were 15, 15 of them. I don't know what the Prosecution's intentions are as to expert witnesses, but there are some categories that seem to me necessary ones. There will be at least one military expert witness who will have to come to explain the structure of the VRS and its command. So this is a typical military expert witness. But there are also issues connected with shellings, with technical issues, as to the type, the calibre of shells, their velocity, their trajectory, the angle and so on. So I believe it will be necessary to have an expert witness to testify on this. Of course, it is up to the Prosecution to decide whether they want to have further expert witnesses. I'm talking about these expert witnesses because an expert witness is useful to answer the questions you will put to them. It's important for the Prosecution. But for the Defence expert witnesses, we also have a very important issue which is the report that they are supposed to draw up and they will seek to admit, because if a witness is called and their report is not admitted, it's a waste of time for everybody. So it's important to choose the right expert witness. Something else that I will now mention. I saw in other trial proceedings that there is a practice which I personally find to be prohibited. It's the issue of the witness who is going to testify. I'm talking now, for example, about a Prosecution witness. The Defence team will hear that Mr. So-and-so will come as a Prosecution witness, and just before that person testifies or the night before the Defence will meet with the witness. That's something that I don't find normal. Personally, I believe that a part -- a witness called by a party should only be interviewed by the calling party. If the other party wishes to put questions to that witness, they should do so publicly, in a public hearing, during cross-examination of the said witness. I know that this has been admitted in other Trial Chambers. I am against it personally. Another point that I should bring to the attention of the Prosecution. In some trials we do see that the Prosecution continues inquiring, investigating during the trial proceedings. Let me take an example, the Galic case. Following the actual trial proceedings, after the trial proceedings as such, the Prosecution sought to admit new exhibits whilst the trial was over. The proceedings were over, and exhibits were added, and that's not normal in my view. If the investigation continues during the trial proceedings, in my view the Trial Chamber should be informed of it, and it should not be a fait accompli for the Trial Chamber. If there is an application or motion to reopen the case, the Prosecution case, because in the meantime the Prosecution would have hold of -- of exhibits, it would like to call new witnesses, whilst the Trial Chamber has not even been informed of such intention. Personally speaking once again, I am not in favour of this type of sort of ongoing investigation, when to me when trial proceedings commence the investigation is over but for exceptional circumstances. If, for example, the Prosecution were to receive exhibits from some authority, some likely piece of evidence. But for that sort of cases. Some investigations started as early as ten years ago. If Prosecution investigations continue even ten years later, there could be real problems if that were to be the case. And I think the decisions were issued by Trial Chambers in this respect. They turned down Prosecution applications for the production of new evidence because the due diligence had failed to be applied. Mr. Stamp, earlier on you mentioned protective measures. It can be indeed that some witnesses would seek protective measures. It is the very fundamental right of any witness to obtain such protective measures. There are two ways to go about them. There is the usual way which is an application by the Prosecution for protective measures, and this of course takes a lot of time. You have to write submissions, argue the case in court, and then there is a written decision by the Trial Chamber. But there is also another way of proceeding which myself and other colleagues used in another case. It is a procedure whereby there is no initial written submission, but just before the hearing or before the testimony the -- or before the hearing the Prosecution or the party tells the senior legal officer whether the witness is seeking protective measures and what kind of protective measures. Then when everybody's in court the blinds are pulled down and there is a discussion. The Trial Chamber seeks to know from the calling party what the objective grounds are for such protective measures. I think it is very practical as a way of proceeding. It really enables us to save a lot of time. Some witnesses may have already been granted protective measures. And so I ask the Prosecution to really be very careful and check that such witnesses -- or whether they were already protected witnesses before, because I've noted already that there are witnesses who are called to testify while they have been under protective measures in another case and the Prosecution didn't know about it. It's unbelievable, but it can happen. So now that we've got all this sort of electronic system, we should know whether a given person was granted protect measures in another case previously. There is also the issue of video-conferences. You may have old people, people who are ill or unable to come to The Hague. So they can't come. Therefore, it may be necessary to organise video-conferences. It is, of course, up to the Prosecution for the Prosecution witnesses and to the Defence for Defence witnesses to let the Trial Chamber know in time, because it is quite a heavy operation. It requires the Registry to be quite active, and we need ample time to organise such video-conferences. So you must let us know in time so as to organise such video-conferences. There is also another point. It is about possible agreements between the two parties as to facts that are not going to be controversial. So some things are not challenged by the Defence. Of course, the agreed facts are mentioned by the Rules. It is then incumbent on the Prosecution to address and approach the Defence and say, These are the facts that I would like to put to the Trial Chamber with your agreement as facts which will not have to be discussed in court because they're not challenged by the Defence. Experience shows that in some cases there are lists of facts that are not disputed, and in some other cases nothing is agreed upon. It is a complete failure, then, in this respect. But the Prosecution will look into this because this matter is quite a relevant one in trial proceedings. Something else now. First I'll ask to move to closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Private session, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're back in open session. And I have a list of items which can be looked into in the next Status Conferences so as to have the best trial proceedings possible. So as to what I have just said, do you have any observations, Mr. Stamp? Do you have any comments? Then I'll give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no comments in respect to the last comments made by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any comments or questions, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do not. I don't know if we're coming to the close of the Status Conference, because I'm wondering whether you be giving the floor to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet. Not yet. We're not at the end of it yet because I have to turn to the accused. General --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. I wasn't expecting you to allow the accused to speak right now, but I do have a request that I would like to address to the Court so that the accused, General Milosevic, will not have to explain it. In the month of June, he received a very good computer from his family, which in the light of the way we will proceed with this trial is essential to him in order to prepare his defence. It seems, though, that this is a very advanced capacity computer and has more than it is supposed to have as far as its capacities, and regardless of a number interventions, the Registry has still not made it possible for him to actually use the computer. General Milosevic has agreed for this computer to be downgraded so that he could finally get it and start using it to work with it. So I would just like to request the Trial Chamber to perhaps exert some influence on the Registry so that this matter could be resolved as soon as possible so that he could start using this computer in order to prepare for his defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if my understanding is correct, he received a computer from his family but he can't use it yet because the Registry has not given him the computer. Is that how things stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is it exactly, Your Honour, because they believe that this computer has wireless capacity and it is then essential to remove some components of the computer, which he agrees with, so that he could actually have it to use it in order to be able to proceed with his Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I'll talk to the registry about it. I'll send a memo on the issue so as to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as soon as I have a reply, a response from the Registry, I'll forward it to you and to the Prosecution. It should be settled very quickly. It's all but normal for an accused to be able to use a computer, precisely to be able to access his file. I mean, we are now in the era of electronics, and the rights of the accused must be respected in that framework, and at the very least he or she should have a computer. So I'll look into this straight after this hearing is over. General, I have two questions for you regarding detention conditions. Is everything going okay? Do you receive visits? Do you have special requests? I'm not talking now about the computer because that's been dealt with, but are you satisfied with the detention conditions or do you have remarks or comments? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for the opportunity to speak and to respond to your questions. All I can say is that there are no problems of the kind that you are asking me about. My detention is proceeding in the usual way. Everything is in accordance with the rules, and I do not have any particular questions or anything particular to say about this. Despite this problem with the computer, the laptop being dealt with, I would still like to say that something was not quite right there. However, I will be very happy were you to request that this question be resolved as soon as possible. Of course we cannot force anything. It has to be all the way it's supposed to be. But I don't have anything else more to say on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your answer. The second question I have to put to you concerns your health. Do you have any problems? Do you have regular visits by the Detention Unit doctor? Anything to say in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything in particular to state on that matter. All I can say is that everything is fine on the whole. I didn't even intend to say anything about it because I know last time when I mentioned how quick the intervention was and how fast my operation was organised, and I said this with the best of intentions, but the media had a different approach to that. So I was a little surprised. However, everything is all right, and I'm hoping that what I state here will be conveyed in the spirit that it was made. Again, I thank you for the opportunity to speak, and I repeat that I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want to mention something else? Do you have questions to put to me? I'm here to meet all your concerns. Do you have any special questions to me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The key matter is the one that was discussed just now. All that has to do with that, of course, interests me specifically, but I think that today I received a lot of information which indicates to me how the proceedings will continue. As for my expectations, if they are not met in the context of what was discussed today, then I will mention that if that time should come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General. Please sit down. We are coming to a close. I shall ask both parties if they have other questions. Mr. Stamp, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing to add. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has nothing to add at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As I said, before coming to a close, I am going to issue a Scheduling Order related to 65 ter (E). I shall see you again very soon. I'm not going to wait 120 days to do so. I think I should be seeing you within a month, or a month and a staff, so that we can really take stock of the situation and to see how ready this case is. So in December there should be a new Status Conference. I want to be really involved personally in this preparation, even though I may not be the Presiding Judge later on or even be in this Chamber, but I want to ensure that those who are going to hear the case have available a file which is prepared perfectly and makes it possible to have the best possible trial proceedings. In the meantime, of course, I do invite the Defence to keep meeting with Mr. Stamp, because such meetings often make it possible to solve problems, are really useful for everybody and are also in the interests of justice. Thank you very much. See you very soon.
